summary: A slight revision and extension of RFC 1048 that defines vendor information tags carried in BOOTP replies, the way a booting machine learns settings from a server. This edition adds tag 13 for the boot file size. It was replaced by RFC 1395, RFC 1497 and RFC 1533.

eli5.summary: When a computer wakes up it knows nothing. This is a list of little labeled notes a helper computer can hand over, such as the size of the file it needs to start.

questions: what is the bootp magic cookie
subtitle: Tagged configuration data that a boot server sends to machines waking up on a network.

tldr.problem: A booting machine needs network settings like its IP address, DNS servers, and a boot file location, but the basic BOOTP protocol only handles a few of these.
tldr.mechanism: BOOTP vendor information extensions define a set of tagged fields that a server includes in its reply, carrying any combination of settings the client needs.
tldr.outcome: This was replaced by DHCP (RFC 1533), which provides the same service in a more modern way.

today: RFC 1084 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1395, RFC 1497, and especially RFC 1533 (DHCP), which replaced BOOTP with a more flexible protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
This RFC revises and extends RFC 1048, adding support for new tagged fields in BOOTP vendor information. As networks grew, booting machines needed to learn many settings beyond what the basic BOOTP protocol provided: not just an IP address and boot file location, but also subnet masks, gateway addresses, time servers, DNS servers, and more. Rather than changing the BOOTP protocol itself (which would risk breaking existing implementations), this RFC defines a vendor information field inside the BOOTP reply where these extra settings can be placed using a simple tagging scheme.

The main driver is administrative simplicity: without these extensions, each booting host would need a unique configuration file, leading to chaos at scale. By centralizing and categorizing configuration data, administrators can group hosts into classes and maintain just a few configuration templates.
sections.eli5: The boot server needs to tell new computers lots of information at once. This RFC is like a post office that labels each piece of mail with a little tag so the computer knows what it is.

sections.title: The Vendor Information Format
sections.content:
The BOOTP reply packet includes a 64-byte vendor information field. This RFC specifies how to organize that field as a sequence of tagged items. The first 4 bytes are a magic cookie with the value 99.130.83.99 in network byte order; this tells the booting machine that the data following uses the standard tag format, not some proprietary scheme.

Each tag consists of a 1-octet tag number, a 1-octet length (except for fixed-size fields), and then the data. This design lets clients safely skip tags they do not understand. Importantly, the 64-byte limit is a hard constraint: administrators must choose carefully which configuration items to include for each boot scenario, omitting non-essential data like hostname or quote-of-the-day server addresses if space is tight.
sections.eli5: The 64 bytes is like a postcard. The first 4 bytes say "this is using the standard labels". Then each label says "I am tag 3" or "I am tag 6" and how many bytes of information follow.

sections.title: Standard Tags
sections.content:
This RFC defines tags 0 through 13 for generic configuration, plus reserved tags 128 through 254 for vendor-specific use. Key tags include: Tag 1 (subnet mask), Tag 2 (time offset in seconds from UTC), Tag 3 (gateway addresses), Tag 4 (time servers), Tag 6 (DNS servers), Tag 12 (hostname), and Tag 13 (boot file size in 512-byte blocks). Tag 255 marks the end of useful data. Tag 0 is padding, used to align data to word boundaries if the target hardware requires it.

The variable-length tags (3 through 11, and others) can carry multiple items of the same type: for example, tag 3 might list three gateway addresses, each 4 bytes, so its length would be 12 bytes total. This single RFC adds Tag 13, the boot file size, which is the main revision from RFC 1048.
sections.eli5: Each tag is like a letter in a word. Tag 1 means "subnet mask", tag 6 means "DNS servers". The machine reads the tag number, sees how long the data is, and grabs it.

sections.title: Comparison and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC acknowledges an alternative approach: instead of BOOTP telling a booting machine where every service is, the machine could simply multicast directly to each service group it needs (like "find me a time server"). Multicasting would reduce dependency on a centralized BOOTP database and potentially lower packet traffic. However, multicasting was not widely implemented at the time, so BOOTP extensions provided a practical solution for the Internet as it existed.

A key practical constraint is the 64-byte limit on vendor data. Administrators are advised not to include every possible configuration item, but rather to include only what the target host class truly needs. Non-critical items (like hostname or quote-of-the-day server) can be located later using service-discovery protocols.
sections.eli5: The BOOTP server could broadcast "is anyone a time server?" and wait for answers. But it is faster to just tell the machine "your time server is here", so that is what this does.

fields.name: Magic Cookie
fields.desc: Fixed value 99.130.83.99 (0x63825363); indicates standard tag format is in use.

fields.name: Tagged Items
fields.desc: Variable-length tags (tag, length, value) for subnet mask, gateways, servers, hostname, boot file size, etc.

fields.name: End Tag and Padding
fields.desc: Tag 255 marks end of usable data; remainder filled with zeros.
